topicTitle: Working with Web APIs: Fetch API & REST

lessons.title: Client-Server Communication & RESTful API Architecture
lessons.description: Understand how web apps communicate with servers using HTTP requests and REST conventions.

sections.heading: How client-server communication works
paragraphs: Web applications follow a client-server model. Your browser (client) sends HTTP requests to a server, which responds with data. REST is a set of conventions for structuring these requests.
list: Client sends a request → Server processes it → Server sends a response
HTTP methods define the action: GET (read), POST (create), PUT (update), DELETE (remove)
Resources are identified by URLs: /api/users, /api/posts/1
Data is exchanged as JSON (typically)

codeExamples.heading: REST API conventions
codeExamples.code:
GET    /api/users          → list all users
GET    /api/users/1        → get user #1
POST   /api/users          → create a new user
PUT    /api/users/1        → update user #1
DELETE /api/users/1        → delete user #1
explanation: GET retrieves data — it should never change server state.
POST creates new resources on the server.
PUT replaces or updates an existing resource.
DELETE removes a resource.
URLs use nouns for resources, HTTP methods for actions.

practice.task: List 5 REST API endpoints for a blog application (posts, comments, users). Write the HTTP method and URL for each CRUD operation.
hints: Each resource gets its own URL pattern.
Use HTTP methods to indicate the action.

keyTakeaways: REST is a convention for structuring HTTP requests and responses.
HTTP methods map to CRUD operations: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.
URLs represent resources, not actions.
JSON is the standard data format for API communication.
lessons.challenge: Design a REST API for a to-do list app with endpoints for lists, tasks, and users.

lessons.title: Sending Requests with fetch() & Parsing Responses (.json())
lessons.description: Use the fetch API to make HTTP requests and parse JSON responses.

sections.heading: The fetch API
paragraphs: fetch() is the modern way to make HTTP requests. It returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object — you then parse the body as JSON or text.
list: fetch(url) — returns a Promise resolving to a Response object
response.json() — parses the body as JSON (also returns a Promise)
response.text() — parses the body as plain text
response.ok — true if status is 200–299

codeExamples.heading: Basic fetch usage
explanation: fetch() returns a Response Promise — not the data yet.
You must call .json() (or .text()) to parse the body.
Always check response.ok — fetch doesn't reject on HTTP errors.
Both fetch and .json() are async — use await on each.

practice.task: Fetch a list of posts from a public API (jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts) and log the title of each post.

keyTakeaways: fetch() returns a Promise that resolves to a Response object.
Always check response.ok — fetch doesn't reject on HTTP errors.
Call .json() or .text() to parse the response body.
Both fetch and body parsing are async — chain with await.
lessons.challenge: Fetch a specific post by ID and its comments, displaying them on the page.

lessons.title: Configuring HTTP Verbs: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE
lessons.description: Use fetch options to send different types of HTTP requests with custom methods.

sections.heading: Fetch options
paragraphs: The second argument to fetch() is an options object where you specify the HTTP method, headers, body and other request details.
list: method — HTTP verb: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH
headers — object with request headers
body — data to send (must be a string for JSON)
JSON.stringify() is required for sending JSON data

codeExamples.heading: POST, PUT, DELETE with fetch
explanation: POST requests need a body — stringify objects with JSON.stringify().
Always set Content-Type header to application/json for JSON data.
DELETE requests typically don't need a body.
PUT replaces the entire resource — PATCH updates individual fields.

practice.task: Create a new post using fetch with the POST method to jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts. Log the response to verify creation.

keyTakeaways: Specify the HTTP method in fetch options: GET, POST, PUT, DELETE.
Always set Content-Type header when sending JSON data.
Use JSON.stringify() to convert objects to JSON for the request body.
GET is the default — other methods require explicit configuration.
lessons.challenge: Build a CRUD interface for posts: create, read, update, and delete — all using fetch with the correct HTTP methods.

lessons.title: Handling Request Headers & Payload Data
lessons.description: Set custom headers for authentication, content types and other metadata.

sections.heading: Request headers
paragraphs: Headers carry metadata about the request — content type, authorization tokens, custom application data and more.
list: Content-Type — tells the server what format the body is in
Authorization — carries authentication tokens (Bearer tokens)
Accept — tells the server what format you want back
Custom headers: any string key is valid

codeExamples.heading: Headers and authentication
explanation: Authorization header carries the Bearer token for authenticated requests.
Accept header tells the server what response format you prefer.
FormData handles file uploads — the browser sets the correct Content-Type.
Never set Content-Type manually for FormData — the browser does it with the boundary.

practice.task: Make a fetch request with custom headers: Authorization (Bearer token) and Accept (application/json). Log the response.
hints: Set headers as an object: { "Authorization": "Bearer mytoken", "Accept": "application/json" }.
Pass headers in the fetch options: fetch(url, { headers }).
Always include error handling for 401/403 responses.

keyTakeaways: Headers carry metadata: content type, authentication, custom data.
Always set Content-Type when sending JSON data.
Authorization header is used for Bearer token authentication.
Use FormData for file uploads — don't set Content-Type manually.
lessons.challenge: Build a function that sends a POST request with JSON body, custom authorization header, and handles 401 errors specifically.

lessons.title: Request Cancellation via AbortController API
lessons.description: Cancel ongoing fetch requests when they're no longer needed — essential for search-as-you-type.

sections.heading: Why cancel requests?
paragraphs: When a user types in a search box, each keystroke fires a new request. Without cancellation, old requests still complete and their results may overwrite newer ones. AbortController lets you cancel stale requests.
list: new AbortController() — creates a controller
controller.signal — a signal object passed to fetch
controller.abort() — cancels the request
Aborted fetches reject with an AbortError

codeExamples.heading: Cancelling fetch requests
explanation: Each new search cancels the previous request with abort().
The abort signal is passed to fetch via the options object.
Aborted fetches throw an AbortError — catch it specifically.
This pattern is essential for search-as-you-type functionality.

practice.task: Implement a search input that cancels the previous request when a new character is typed. Use AbortController.
hints: Create a controller variable outside the search function.
Call controller.abort() at the start of each new search.
Pass signal: controller.signal in the fetch options.
Catch AbortError specifically to suppress cancellation errors.

keyTakeaways: AbortController cancels ongoing fetch requests.
Pass the signal to fetch: { signal: controller.signal }.
Aborted requests throw an AbortError — catch and handle it.
Essential for search-as-you-type and other rapid-fire request patterns.
lessons.challenge: Build a type-ahead search that cancels requests older than 500ms using AbortController and setTimeout.
